results.corrected_title: European Commission opens consultation on AI Act rules for enforcement proceedings and penalties (Articles 75c/75d)
results.corrected_summary: On 12 October 2026 the European Commission published a draft implementing regulation, Ares(2026)9589403, setting procedural rules for AI Act enforcement proceedings under Articles 75c and 75d. These articles were inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. The draft covers access to the file, protection of business secrets and confidential information, five-year limitation periods for imposing and enforcing fines and periodic penalty payments, and digital transmission of documents. Feedback is open until 9 November 2026, and the Commission plans to adopt the rules in Q4 2026.
key_facts: Applies to operators of AI systems under Article 75(1): AI systems built on a general-purpose AI model from the same provider or group, and AI systems that are, or are part of, very large online platforms or search engines designated under the DSA
Access to the file only after preliminary findings; unredacted material only for named external lawyers, economists and technical experts
Five-year limitation period for fines, restarted by investigative steps, with an absolute ceiling of 10 years
Feedback window 12 October to 9 November 2026; adoption planned for Q4 2026
results.issues: The CMS source in the candidate (dated 20 March 2026) is about a different, earlier draft: the March 2026 draft on evaluations and enforcement for general-purpose AI model providers, with feedback that closed 9 April 2026. It does not support this item and has been removed. The Commission page did not render through fetch; the Ares number, the 12 Oct to 9 Nov window and the Q4 2026 adoption come from search snippets of that page and from PPC Land. LexisNexis (12 Oct) confirms the articles and the content.

results.corrected_title: EU member states back Ireland's Dublin Declaration on Trusted, Safe and Sovereign AI
results.corrected_summary: At the International AI Summit at the RDS in Dublin, a flagship event of Ireland's EU Council presidency, Ireland won backing from EU member states for the Dublin Declaration on Trusted, Safe and Sovereign Artificial Intelligence. The non-binding political declaration commits participating countries to cooperate on AI safety, resilience and governance, to invest in skills, research and digital infrastructure, and to reduce critical technological dependencies. Ireland's announcement does not list all signatories, but press reports say Italy and Spain are missing from the signature pages.
key_facts: Presented at the International AI Summit at the RDS, Dublin, on 14 October 2026, during Ireland's EU Council presidency
Full title in the government text: Dublin Declaration on Trusted, Safe and Sovereign Artificial Intelligence (the PDF uses 'Trustworthy')
Political declaration, not legally binding; Minister of State Niamh Smyth called it 'a strong political signal'
Commitments include AI safety and governance cooperation, skills, research, digital infrastructure, support for European AI companies and reducing critical dependencies
Italy and Spain reportedly did not sign; Niamh Smyth signed for Ireland

best_source.name: Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (Ireland)

results.issues: The candidate says the signatory list was 'not published', but TechCentral reports that the declaration has signature pages, with Italy and Spain absent. The exact number of signatories is still unconfirmed. The summit date of 14 October is inferred from the press release date (14 Oct) and from TechCentral's 'this past Wednesday' in an article dated 16 Oct. Sources disagree on the title wording ('Trusted' vs 'Trustworthy').

results.corrected_title: Ofcom narrows its X/Grok investigation after porn restrictions for UK users, but concerns remain about hate and terror content
results.corrected_summary: On 14 October 2026 Ofcom said SpaceXAI (formerly xAI) now blocks UK users from viewing, generating or sharing pornographic content through Grok's standalone image tools, and stops companion chatbots such as 'Ani' from sexually explicit conversations. X also fixed a gap that let unverified accounts see age-restricted porn. Ofcom is therefore dropping the child-protection strand and has moved its Online Safety Act investigation, opened in January 2026, into a new phase on X's illegal-content duties and its reporting and complaints systems. Ofcom also said it still has concerns about how well X removes illegal hate and terror content, even though X met its targets for reviewing reports.
key_facts: Ofcom update published 14 October 2026; investigation opened in January 2026 over Grok-generated sexualised deepfakes
UK users are blocked from viewing, generating or sharing porn via Grok's image tools; companion bots such as 'Ani' are barred from explicit chats
Ofcom is not pursuing the child-protection assessment after X fixed age-verification gaps; it now focuses on illegal content and reporting/complaints systems
X's first quarterly report: reported posts reviewed within 24 hours on average and at least 85% assessed within 48 hours, but Ofcom still doubts illegal posts are actually being removed
No breach finding yet; if Ofcom finds reasonable grounds, it will issue a provisional view before any final decision
results.issues: The Ofcom page returned HTTP 403 and could not be opened directly; the facts are confirmed by Reuters (via BusinessDay) and The Next Web, both dated 14 October 2026. Small precision point: the porn block applies to Grok's standalone image-generation tools.
